```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4.5,
                      out.width = "80%")
show_file <- function(path) cat(readLines(path), sep = "\n")
```

## Why this check

A matched study estimates the propensity score with one model, usually logistic regression.
Another model that fits about as well, such as Bayesian additive regression trees or a
generalized random forest, can rank the patients differently, give some treated patients
different untreated partners, and so change the matched design. `propsens` describes how much the
design depends on that choice, **without looking at outcomes**, so it can be run at the design
stage, next to the usual balance table. Every summary describes the study as a whole.

**Status of the evidence.** These diagnostics have been studied in the author's simulations and
benchmark analyses; a methods paper is in preparation. No peer-reviewed evaluation exists yet,
and no thresholds for a "large" value exist yet. Report the output as a description of how much
the matched design depends on the choice of propensity model, not as a validated check.

For a short overview, see [propsens at a glance](at-a-glance.html)
(`vignette("at-a-glance", package = "propsens")`). For the method explained one idea at a time
with a real clinical example, see [How propsens works, step by step](how-it-works.html)
(`vignette("how-it-works", package = "propsens")`).

## One call on your own `matchit` object

```{r match}
library(propsens)
data("lalonde", package = "MatchIt")

matched <- MatchIt::matchit(
  treat ~ age + educ + race + married + nodegree + re74 + re75,
  data = lalonde, method = "nearest", distance = "glm", link = "linear.logit",
  replace = TRUE
)
```

`propensity_sensitivity()` reads the formula and the matching options from the object, refits
the propensity model with logistic regression, Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) and a
generalized random forest (GRF) (three seeds for each tree algorithm, cross-fitted scores),
re-matches with the same options, applies the quality gate and computes the diagnostics, with 20
bootstrap refits of the logistic model. These are the defaults, and the model set to use in an
analysis:

```{r defaults, eval = FALSE}
sensitivity <- propensity_sensitivity(matched)
sensitivity
```

It takes about a minute on these data, so the output below was computed once with the script
`data-raw/lalonde_default_output.R` and is shown as text:

```{r defaults-output, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
show_file("lalonde-default-print.txt")
```

**What this output says.** On these data no refitted model reaches the balance limit: every one
of them has a largest standardized mean difference above 0.25 after matching, so fewer than two
models pass the gate. The function raises an R warning and the output opens with it: there is no
set of similarly good models to compare, and every number describes all seven models. Your own
model (the `glm` of the `matchit` object) is within the balance limit, but it is judged on
balance only and is an in-sample score, while the refitted logistic regression is cross-fitted and
judged on both fit and balance; your own model is never one of the models compared. When the gate keeps none of
the refitted models, as here, the next step is to revisit the matching design (covariates,
caliper, replacement), not to read the summaries.

The result also depends on `seed`. `seed_sensitivity()` reruns the call with several seeds:

```{r seeds, eval = FALSE}
seed_sensitivity(matched, seeds = 1:3)
```

```{r seeds-output, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
show_file("lalonde-default-seeds.txt")
```

With `seed = 1` every model is used (fallback); with seeds 2 and 3 the gate keeps only BART fits,
so rank disagreement then measures only BART's seed noise (and the function warns). None of the
three seeds gives a kept set from two or more algorithms. Report every row.

## A simulated example where the gate keeps several algorithms

On lalonde none of the three seeds gave a kept set from two or more algorithms. The data below
are **simulated** with `simulate_example_data()` (Scenario 1: six normal covariates, a logistic
treatment model, 1,000 patients), to show the output when the gate keeps models from several
algorithms. It was computed once with `data-raw/simulated_default_output.R`:

```{r simulated, eval = FALSE}
simulated <- simulate_example_data(n = 1000, scenario = "S1", seed = 1)
propensity_sensitivity(treat ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6, data = simulated)
```

```{r simulated-output, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
show_file("simulated-default-print.txt")
```

```{r simulated-seeds, eval = FALSE}
seed_sensitivity(treat ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6, seeds = 1:3, data = simulated)
```

```{r simulated-seeds-output, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
show_file("simulated-default-seeds.txt")
```

All three seeds keep models from three algorithms; every row is reported.

## The printed lines, on a faster run

So that this vignette builds quickly, the runs below use the faster model set (logistic
regression, random forests and gradient boosting), fewer seeds and fewer refits. The output has
the same structure.

```{r sensitivity}
sensitivity <- propensity_sensitivity(
  matched, algorithms = c("logistic_regression", "random_forest", "gradient_boosting"),
  seeds = 1:2, n_trees = 100, bootstrap_samples = 5
)
sensitivity
```

How to read the printed lines, in their order:

- **WARNING (when present).** Fewer than two models passed the gate: every model is used, and
  the values describe all models, not a kept set.
- **1. Quality gate.** How many models were kept, from how many algorithms, and the rule: a model
  is kept only if its cross-fitted log-loss is within 5 % of the best model's and its largest
  standardized mean difference on main terms after matching is at most 0.10 above the best
  model's and at most 0.25 (`balance_rule = "absolute"` uses a fixed 0.10 instead). When the
  kept models are seeds of one algorithm, a block says so (and the function warns): the
  disagreement is then seed noise. The excluded models are listed with the reason, then the
  share of treated patients kept by each kept model (below 100 % only with a caliper).
  `r if (!"logistic_regression_1" %in% sensitivity$summary$models_used) "In this run the refitted logistic regression, the analyst's usual kind of model, is not kept: another algorithm fitted or balanced clearly better here, and the summaries describe the kept models only." else "In this run the refitted logistic regression is one of the kept models."`
- **2. Rank disagreement (primary).** For each patient, the standard deviation over the kept
  models of the patient's percentile rank (0 to 1) of the propensity score; averaged over treated
  patients. 0 means every kept model orders the patients the same way. Read it for the study as
  a whole. It depends on how many seeds each kept algorithm has; the next line, **equal weight
  per algorithm** (exploratory), counts each algorithm once.
- **Between/within-algorithm ratio (exploratory).** Disagreement between algorithms divided by
  disagreement between seeds of the same algorithm. With three seeds per algorithm, seed noise
  alone gives a ratio of about 0.4; larger values point to disagreement between algorithms
  beyond seed noise. `NA` when no kept algorithm has two seeds.
- **Pair instability (exploratory).** How often the kept models choose different untreated
  partners, with its maximum for the number of kept models. It is high whenever many untreated
  patients have similar scores, even when the models agree.
- **Bootstrap rank instability (descriptive).** The standard deviation of a patient's
  percentile rank over bootstrap refits of the logistic model, averaged over treated patients:
  sampling noise of one model. Report it next to rank disagreement.
- **3. Balance spread (descriptive).** The range of the largest standardized mean difference on
  main terms across the kept models.
- **Control spread (descriptive).** For each treated patient, how different the untreated
  partners chosen by the different models are, in units of a typical distance between a treated
  patient and its partner.
- **Your own model.** The model of the `matchit` object, judged on balance only.
- **Matching.** The matching settings and the target: with a caliper, the estimand is the effect
  in the retained treated patients.

`summary()` gives every study-level number for the kept models and for every model, each with
its label, the table of models and the reasons each model was or was not kept:

```{r summary}
summary(sensitivity)
```

The per-patient table is available with `as.data.frame()`. Its columns describe how the
disagreement is spread over the patients; they are not flags for individual patients.

```{r patients}
head(as.data.frame(sensitivity))
```

## The three plots

**Patients.** One point per treated patient: rank disagreement across the kept models (x)
against the scaled control spread (y). It describes how the disagreement is spread over the
treated patients; individual points should not be read as flags for individual patients. Colour
shows whether the patient's logistic score lies outside the range of the untreated patients'
scores.

```{r plot-patients}
plot(sensitivity, type = "patients")
```

**Models.** The four balance statistics after matching, one panel each, one row per model, each
axis starting at 0. Filled points are kept by the quality gate, hollow points are not; your own
model is drawn in its own colour. The dashed line is the balance limit of the gate.

```{r plot-models, fig.height = 5.5}
plot(sensitivity, type = "models")
```

**Recurrence.** The pair recurrence: the share of kept models (or bootstrap refits) that choose a
treated patient's most common untreated partner. One minus its mean over treated patients across
the kept models is pair instability (exploratory). Low recurrence is expected when untreated
patients are dense, even when the models agree.

```{r plot-recurrence}
plot(sensitivity, type = "recurrence")
```

## Without a `matchit` object

The same diagnostic runs on a formula and a data frame; the matching options are then
arguments (without replacement, order "largest", no caliper by default):

```{r formula, eval = FALSE}
propensity_sensitivity(treat ~ age + educ + race + married + nodegree + re74 + re75,
                       data = lalonde)
```

## What to do with the result

1. If a warning appears, revisit the matching design first.
2. Rerun with two or three values of `seed` (`seed_sensitivity()`) and report every row.
3. Show the models plot next to your balance table, and choose the design by balance, never by
   the outcome.
4. Decide before looking at outcomes whether you will report the effect estimate under each
   kept model, and then report all of them.

The check does not detect unmeasured confounding and is not a fix: it describes how much your
matched design depends on one modelling choice. A small value is not evidence that the estimate
is unbiased.
